body:
After agreement with @thesimplekid I pass here our short conversation on the topic:

>  Have you though about splicing at all? Thats kinda how I though liquidity management with mints between onchain and ln would work well. Though I know its not that well supported yet lnd not at all and not many cln and ldk mints out there. 
> 
> I think what you suggest in an interesting idea and I don't think would be too hard on the mint side. I think showing it to users would be harder though maybe most users would just not really notice this and only the special actors interested in doing the arbitrageur would have to worry about it. I think that is a potential down side as well as it needs these special actors but these days maybe thats just someones bot if the profit incentive is there.


> Thanks for pointing it out!
> 
> I see now that splicing can payout any onchain address - did not know that. So that might be indeed an additional option to weight against.
> Economically when splicing the costs are fully beared by the mint operator (as he is the one initiating it).
> 
> The question then is if we'd accept some added complexity to the protocol with aim to create a possible market incentives to mint ecash - and let some kid's bots doing the work. 
> 
> I still lean in favour of it, because it can compete in aggregate with splicing, normal transaction should be a little cheaper then 2 of 2 splicing one, and is really unique to how ecash works.

## Since 8 October

- Transcript: quote inputs (0x12) commit their lock key and `amount_issued`; blinded outputs (0x21) commit `SHA256(B_)`. Vectors regenerated.
- NUT-04: derived quote ids, `tagged_hash("Cashu_QuoteId", id_preimage)`; NUT-13 type 0x05 derives the preimage.
- NUT-22 request target is the path relative to the mint URL.
- Tighter malformed-input rules (witness entries, preimage length, spend info, NUT-13 scope and counter, NUT-28 slot index).

## Since 8 October

- Change quote ids derive from an `id_preimage` the wallet supplies, or, when it is omitted, from the transaction's inputs (new vector).
- With a melt, the melt quote is the transaction's record; the separate record and its route are gone.
- A pending input quote refuses other draws (20005).
- NUT-17 `change_mint_quote` kind.

## Since the 7 October review

- The template leaf names destination keys (`dests`) instead of hashing the outputs: every output must be a change quote to a listed key. Amounts and ids are the spender's.
- No time field; a timeout is an `after` leaf beside it.
- Vectors: covenant into two change quotes, and an arbiter escrow.

The one-shot discussion in [the earlier review](https://github.com/cashubtc/nuts/pull/457#discussion_r4209544707) predates two changes: quote inputs now bind `amount_issued` (#443), so each signature authorizes one draw at one state of the quote, and with `dests` any later draw needs fresh signatures and can still only pay listed keys.

Implementation PRs for the vector pinning, to go with cashu-ts#786:

- CDK: cashubtc/cdk#2712 — pins the HTLC example proof (slot layout, receiver derivation at slots 1/2, spendability via both pathways), the V4 token decode/re-encode, and the wallet-level \sign_proofs\ derivation. The vector also caught a real interop bug: CDK was encoding \pe\ as a hex string on the CBOR path instead of a 33-byte bstr, so it could not decode spec-compliant P2BK V4 tokens (and vice versa); that is fixed in the PR.
- Nutshell: cashubtc/nutshell#1214 — pins the same vectors at the core, wallet (\_derive_p2bk_signing_keys\) and token layers. Receiver-side slot numbering was already correct there.

One spec-level observation while pinning the token byte-for-byte: the NUT-28 example V4 token orders the top-level CBOR map \m, u, t\, while the NUT-00 example tokens (pinned byte-for-byte by existing Nutshell tests) use \	, d, m, u\. CBOR maps are unordered so both decode everywhere, but the two test files are not byte-consistent with each other — may be worth aligning or stating key order is non-normative.

**minibits-cash:** So when minting onchain, cdk can present address that splices-in to fund your side of some channel? As of what I see now it's definitely onchain where the liquidity is short.

**thesimplekid:** Cdk but presets a normal onchain address user sends to (tx 1) then once received its does a splice (tx 2) and only issues the ecash after tx 2 and for amount minus fee of tx 2. It does require 2 txs and the user has to pay these so thats not the best. However, it does pass the fee burden onto the user in the most honest way as its the fee they force the mint to incur. 

This is similar to what fedimint now does, the federation only has 1 utxo so a user depositing sends to federation (tx 1) then federation consolidates into their 1 utxo (tx 2) and only issues ecash after tx 2 less the cost of the tx 2 fee.

**thesimplekid:** Users are depositing on chain and withdrawing via lighting or the reverse?

**minibits-cash:** Folks are withdrawing on onchain side. So the direction we'd need an incentive for is to mint onchain, or splice-out channels.

> * CDK: [test(nut28): pin the NUT-28 HTLC example vectors; fix pe CBOR bstr encoding cdk#2712](https://github.com/cashubtc/cdk/pull/2712) — pins the HTLC example proof (slot layout, receiver derivation at slots 1/2, spendability via both pathways), the V4 token decode/re-encode, and the wallet-level \sign_proofs\ derivation. The vector also caught a real interop bug: CDK was encoding \pe\ as a hex string on the CBOR path instead of a 33-byte bstr, so it could not decode spec-compliant P2BK V4 tokens (and vice versa); that is fixed in the PR.
> * Nutshell: [test(nut28): pin the NUT-28 HTLC example proof and V4 token vectors nutshell#1214](https://github.com/cashubtc/nutshell/pull/1214) — pins the same vectors at the core, wallet (_derive_p2bk_signing_keys) and token layers. Receiver-side slot numbering was already correct there.

CBOR maps are unordered so both decode everywhere, but the two test files are not byte-consistent with each other — may be worth aligning or stating key order is non-normative.

Nice work @ye0man - and well worth it to squash that CDK bug!

Yes, map key order is non-normative, all three implementations do it differently and the spec has instances encoded from more than one.

Decoders MUST accept any order, and vector tests should compare decoded tokens, not bytes. I added a normative line to NUT-00 in this PR.

I've decided to close this PR that I made

I'm not against hashing the blinded outputs, and am happy for anyone else to advocate for this. It's just that I now have another solution ([Unpoisonable Blinded Outputs](https://gist.github.com/SatsAndSports/6c197ca9da984c1922483e74281d38db)) that fixes the poison issue directly, allowing us to keep using adverserial multi-party e-cash transactions (e.g. Spilman with non-interactive setup)
Folded into https://github.com/cashubtc/nuts/pull/404, which now carries `tests/14-test.md` with these vectors, the HTLC SIG_ALL case included.
